title: Purpose Clauses and Result Constructions
summary: Express intended purposes and actual or designed results precisely. Use in order to, so as to and their negative forms; distinguish infinitive purpose from clauses with so that or in order that; and manage formal result patterns with such that, in such a way as to and such ... that.
learningObjectives: Express affirmative and negative purpose with to-infinitives, in order to, so as to, in order not to and so as not to.
Choose a finite purpose clause with so that or in order that when its subject, tense or modal makes an infinitive unsuitable.
Interpret modal and tense choices in purpose clauses following present and past main clauses without assuming rigid mechanical backshifting.
Distinguish formal result expressions such that, in such a way that, in such a way as to and such + noun phrase + that.

explanation.heading: Affirmative purpose: the ordinary to-infinitive and more explicit alternatives
explanation.body: An infinitive of purpose explains why an action is performed: we moved the meeting to give everyone time. In order to and so as to make that purpose especially clear, and so as to is often relatively formal. The simple to-infinitive is common in speech. Purpose must be distinguished from an infinitive expressing a result or completing another construction; select the form from the meaning, not merely from the adjacent verb.
explanation.example: The volunteers arrived early in order to prepare the hall before the guests entered.

explanation.heading: Negative purpose and contrastive infinitives
explanation.body: To make prevention or avoidance explicit, prefer in order not to or so as not to. A bare not to after an action is often ambiguous or unnatural as a purpose adjunct. Do not apply the same rule mechanically to a contrast such as not to criticise but to help: there, not ... but ... is a paired contrast, and the second infinitive identifies the real intention. In order or so as can optionally precede such contrasting infinitives.
explanation.example: She lowered the microphone so as not to disturb the recording.

explanation.heading: Purpose with a full clause: so that and in order that
explanation.body: When the purpose has its own explicit subject, use a finite clause introduced by so that or the more formal in order that. Modals are frequent: can and will for present or future reference; could and would frequently accompany past-time purposes. They are not mandatory in every purpose clause, but the chosen time reference and meaning must remain coherent. Informal so that may be shortened to so; in order that cannot normally be reduced to in order in this way.
explanation.example: The instructor repeated the directions so that the new students could follow the route.

explanation.heading: Designed or achieved results with such that and in such a way
explanation.body: Such that is comparatively formal and can explain a designed property or a resulting condition: the connections were arranged such that maintenance was straightforward. In such a way that introduces a clause; in such a way as to introduces a to-infinitive. The alternatives often overlap in meaning, but the grammatical complements are not interchangeable. These patterns can describe intended design or actual effects, depending on context.
explanation.example: The sensors were positioned in such a way that visitors could see the display without blocking the entrance.

explanation.heading: Such + noun phrase + that expresses degree and consequence
explanation.body: Such followed by a noun phrase and that expresses the consequence of an unusually strong or noteworthy quality: such a persuasive case that ... . This differs structurally from such that, which does not require an intervening noun phrase. Do not confuse a statement of what actually followed with a statement of what somebody hoped to achieve: a result may be unintended, while purpose is intentional.
explanation.example: It was such a convincing demonstration that several sceptical reviewers changed their minds.

left.label: Negative purpose
left.example: We closed the gate so as not to disturb the nesting birds.
left.note: The gate was closed with an intention to prevent disturbance.

right.label: Contrast of intentions
right.example: We closed the gate not to exclude visitors but to protect the birds.
right.note: Not ... but ... rejects one possible purpose and asserts another.

left.label: Full clause
left.example: The parts were numbered in such a way that volunteers could assemble them.
left.note: That introduces a clause with its own subject and finite verb.

right.label: To-infinitive
right.example: The parts were numbered in such a way as to simplify assembly.
right.note: As to introduces an infinitive describing the intended effect.

examples.sentence: The librarian moved the returns desk to shorten the queue.
examples.note: A plain to-infinitive expresses purpose naturally.

examples.sentence: The runners followed the marked path in order not to damage the gardens.
examples.note: In order not to introduces a negative purpose.

examples.sentence: The organiser emailed a map so that guests would know which entrance to use.
examples.note: Would states the intended outcome from a past viewpoint.

examples.sentence: The gallery was lit such that the inscriptions remained legible from the doorway.
examples.note: Such that introduces the designed result in a formal register.

examples.sentence: There was such intense interest in the workshop that additional sessions were scheduled.
examples.note: Such modifies a noun phrase; that introduces the actual consequence.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The team left a note so as that the next shift could find the equipment.
commonMistakes.correct: The team left a note so that the next shift could find the equipment.
commonMistakes.why: So as to takes an infinitive; so that introduces a finite clause.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The editor removed the name in order not embarrass the author.
commonMistakes.correct: The editor removed the name in order not to embarrass the author.
commonMistakes.why: In order not to requires to before the infinitive embarrass.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The chairs were arranged in such a way as that everyone had a clear view.
commonMistakes.correct: The chairs were arranged in such a way that everyone had a clear view.
commonMistakes.why: Use in such a way that + clause, or in such a way as to + infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: It was such a noisy lecture so that nobody could hear the questions.
commonMistakes.correct: It was such a noisy lecture that nobody could hear the questions.
commonMistakes.why: The result construction is such + noun phrase + that, without so.

studyTips: For each purpose sentence, identify the actor and ask whether the intention can be expressed naturally by one to-infinitive or requires a separate subject in a that-clause.
Contrast negative prevention (in order not to) with rejected motives (not to ... but to ...) by creating two scenarios with different intentions.
Rewrite a designed result three ways: with such that, in such a way that and in such a way as to; check the complement each expression requires.

exercises.prompt: The team covered the instruments because they wanted to prevent dust entering them. Choose the clearest negative-purpose construction.
choices: The team covered the instruments so as not to let dust in.
The team covered the instruments so as that dust would not enter.
The team covered the instruments so as not dust to enter.
exercises.feedback: So as not to + infinitive gives a conventional negative purpose.

exercises.prompt: The caretaker dimmed the lights because she wanted the audience to concentrate on the display. Choose the sentence that keeps the separate subject.
choices: The caretaker dimmed the lights in order the audience concentrating.
The caretaker dimmed the lights so that the audience could concentrate.
The caretaker dimmed the lights so as the audience could concentrate.
exercises.feedback: So that introduces the audience as the subject of a finite purpose clause.

exercises.prompt: Choose the grammatical formal expression of an intended design outcome.
choices: The shelves were spaced in such a way as that allow easy access.
The shelves were spaced in such a way that to allow easy access.
The shelves were spaced in such a way as to allow easy access.
exercises.feedback: In such a way as to is completed by a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence reports an actual consequence using such + noun phrase + that?
choices: The issue caused such confusion that the meeting was extended.
The issue caused such confusion so that the meeting was extended.
The issue caused such that confusion the meeting was extended.
exercises.feedback: Such confusion that introduces the actual result, not an intended aim.

exercises.prompt: "We checked the names twice ___ avoid sending invitations to the wrong people." Supply the three-word phrase beginning with "in" that makes purpose explicit.
exercises.feedback: In order to introduces the intention behind checking.

exercises.prompt: "She kept her voice low ___ wake the sleeping child." Supply the four-word negative-purpose phrase beginning with "so".
exercises.feedback: So as not to + infinitive expresses the intention to prevent waking the child.

exercises.prompt: "The guide repeated the announcement so ___ late arrivals could hear it." Supply the single conjunction component.
exercises.feedback: So that introduces a full purpose clause with a different subject.

exercises.prompt: "The platform was designed ___ that people using wheelchairs could reach every exhibit." Supply the word completing the formal result connector.
exercises.feedback: Such that can introduce a designed property or resulting arrangement.

exercises.prompt: Replace "so as that" with "so that" and preserve the remaining words: "The manager provided printed instructions so as that trainees could work independently."
acceptedAnswers: The manager provided printed instructions so that trainees could work independently.
exercises.feedback: Replace so as that with so that before a full finite clause.

exercises.prompt: Correct the negative purpose: "We reduced the volume so as not disturb neighbouring offices."
acceptedAnswers: We reduced the volume so as not to disturb neighbouring offices.
exercises.feedback: So as not to requires to before the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Correct the mismatch using "in such a way that"; keep the other words: "The display was arranged in such a way as to visitors could find the labels."
acceptedAnswers: The display was arranged in such a way that visitors could find the labels.
exercises.feedback: In such a way that introduces the full clause visitors could find the labels.

exercises.prompt: Correct the noun-phrase result structure: "It was such a useful workshop so that everyone requested a second session."
acceptedAnswers: It was such a useful workshop that everyone requested a second session.
exercises.feedback: Such + noun phrase + that expresses a result without so.

speakingExercises.prompt: Explain the purpose in one sentence. Facts: The team / gather / early / review the route. Start "The team" and use "in order to" with the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The team gathered early in order to review the route.
speakingExercises.feedback: In order to + infinitive introduces the team’s purpose.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a negative purpose. Facts: She / whisper / not wake the baby. Use the past simple and the phrase "so as not to".
acceptedAnswers: She whispered so as not to wake the baby.
speakingExercises.feedback: So as not to explicitly identifies the unwanted outcome being avoided.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a purpose clause with two subjects. Facts: The museum / extend its hours; visitors / can see the exhibition. Begin "The museum" and use "so that".
acceptedAnswers: The museum extended its hours so that visitors could see the exhibition.
speakingExercises.feedback: So that introduces a separate subject; could suits the past purpose.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a present arrangement and intended effect. Facts: They / leave the lights on; the guards / can inspect the building. Start "They" and use "in order that".
acceptedAnswers: They leave the lights on in order that the guards can inspect the building.
speakingExercises.feedback: In order that is the formal connector before a purpose clause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe designed access using "in such a way as to". Facts: The ramp / be built / provide step-free entry. Use the past passive.
acceptedAnswers: The ramp was built in such a way as to provide step-free entry.
speakingExercises.feedback: In such a way as to is followed by an infinitive.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a formal description with "such that". Facts: The signs / be positioned; every passenger / can see them. Begin "The signs" and use the past passive.
acceptedAnswers: The signs were positioned such that every passenger could see them.
speakingExercises.feedback: Such that introduces the designed resulting condition.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express an actual consequence. Facts: It / be / such a persuasive speech; the committee / approve the plan. Use the past simple and "such ... that".
acceptedAnswers: It was such a persuasive speech that the committee approved the plan.
speakingExercises.feedback: Such a persuasive speech that identifies a degree with an actual result.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give two sentences in this order using full forms. First: We / close the window / in order not to / interrupt the recording. Second: We / move the table / so that / everyone / could see the screen. Use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: We closed the window in order not to interrupt the recording. We moved the table so that everyone could see the screen.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first is infinitive negative purpose; the second uses a finite purpose clause.

listeningExercises.audioText: We moved the information desk so that new arrivals could find it more easily.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the intended benefit of moving the desk?
choices: The desk would take up more storage space.
New arrivals would locate the desk more easily.
The desk would be closed during visiting hours.
listeningExercises.feedback: The so that clause specifies improved access for new arrivals.

listeningExercises.audioText: The technician covered the camera so as not to expose the lens to dust.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which outcome was the technician trying to prevent?
choices: Dust reaching the camera lens.
A delay in delivering the camera.
Visitors touching the camera controls.
listeningExercises.feedback: So as not to introduces the problem that the technician wanted to avoid.

listeningExercises.audioText: The ushers arrived early in order to inspect every emergency exit.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the three-word purpose expression beginning with "in".
listeningExercises.feedback: The audio uses in order to immediately before inspect.

listeningExercises.audioText: The notice was printed in such a way that visitors with poor eyesight could read it.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the result of the printing arrangement?
choices: The notice became shorter.
The printing costs were reduced to zero.
The notice was readable by visitors with poor eyesight.
listeningExercises.feedback: In such a way that introduces the readable design outcome.

listeningExercises.audioText: The organisers changed the programme so that the speakers would have longer breaks.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the organisers hope to achieve?
choices: More breaks for the speakers.
Fewer seats in the auditorium.
An earlier closing date for registration.
listeningExercises.feedback: Would have longer breaks states the intended change.

listeningExercises.audioText: It was such a compelling argument that the panel reversed its decision.
listeningExercises.prompt: What actually happened after the argument?
choices: The panel postponed all meetings for a year.
The panel changed its decision.
The panel refused to read the argument.
listeningExercises.feedback: Such ... that introduces the result of the persuasive argument.

listeningExercises.audioText: The team stored the paintings carefully so as not to damage the frames.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the four-word negative-purpose expression beginning with "so".
listeningExercises.feedback: The audible negative purpose is so as not to.

listeningExercises.audioText: The workshop was arranged such that everyone had enough space to move.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word formal result connector beginning with "such".
listeningExercises.feedback: Such that introduces the resulting arrangement.
